lesson.title: England's Foothold on the James River
lesson.summary: Founded in 1607 by investors seeking profit rather than settlers seeking a new life, Jamestown nearly failed multiple times before tobacco cultivation gave England's first permanent North American colony a reason to survive.
lesson.body:
Jamestown existed because a group of London investors believed North America might hold profitable resources the way Spanish America had. In 1606, King James I chartered the Virginia Company of London, a joint stock company that let investors pool money and share risk, exactly the financing model that had eluded earlier English attempts like Roanoke. Three ships, the Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery, carried about one hundred colonists across the Atlantic, and in May 1607 they selected a site on a peninsula along a river they named the James, after the king.

The location was chosen for defense rather than health. Its deep water anchorage let ships dock close to shore, and its distance upriver offered some protection from Spanish patrols, since Spain still regarded the region as within its sphere of claims. But the site was swampy and surrounded by brackish, often contaminated water, and it bred the mosquitoes that carried malaria. Combined with a colonist population weighted toward gentlemen unaccustomed to manual labor and unrealistic hopes of quickly finding gold, the site's poor conditions produced catastrophic death rates in the colony's early years.

The winter of 1609 to 1610, remembered as the starving time, was the low point. Disease, conflict with neighboring Powhatan communities, and a supply fleet delayed by shipwreck left the colony without adequate food, and only a small fraction of the several hundred colonists present survived to spring. Captain John Smith's leadership in 1608, when he imposed strict work requirements on the colony, had briefly improved conditions, but his departure after an injury in 1609 removed that discipline just as the crisis deepened. Survival during these years depended heavily on trade with the Powhatan Confederacy, the powerful network of Algonquian communities in the region, for corn and other food, a relationship that swung between cooperation and open conflict.

What finally secured the colony's future was not gold but tobacco. Around 1612, colonist John Rolfe began cultivating a sweeter strain of tobacco derived from Caribbean varieties, one far more appealing to European tastes than the harsher native Virginia tobacco. Tobacco exports gave the Virginia Company and individual colonists a genuine cash crop, and the colony's population and land under cultivation began expanding steadily as a result. Rolfe's 1614 marriage to Pocahontas, daughter of the Powhatan leader Wahunsenacawh, also brought several years of relative peace between the colony and its indigenous neighbors.

Jamestown's institutions matured alongside its economy. In 1619, the Virginia Company authorized the House of Burgesses, the first representative legislative assembly in English North America, giving colonists a voice in local governance even as the colony remained subject to English oversight. That same year also saw the arrival of the first recorded Africans in English North America, laborers whose presence would eventually reshape Virginia's economy and society. The Virginia Company itself proved commercially unsuccessful and lost its charter in 1624, becoming a royal colony under direct crown control, but by then Jamestown had already demonstrated that English settlement in North America could take root and endure.
